title: Bad Goals Dressed as Good Ones
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that certain goals commonly celebrated in high school culture—top-10 class rank, valedictorian, admission to a prestigious college—are, at the grand scale of a student’s whole life and the public education system, poorly designed goals. He offers five criteria for why: they are scarce (requiring competition for limited spots), they emphasize an external locus of control, they are not strongly correlated with long-term flourishing, they make every academic moment feel make-or-break, and they orient students toward a utilitarian future rather than the present good of learning. The article closes with a call for careful heart-gardening by teachers—light-touch, consistent work to move students toward wiser, more humane definitions of success that locate motivation in the inherent value of learning rather than in the destinations it might fund.
points: Externally competitive goals (class rank, valedictorian, elite college) fail at the grand scale because success depends substantially on factors outside the student’s control—who else is competing, what the admissions committee wants—rather than on the student’s own disciplined choices.

Scarcity is a structural flaw: goals requiring students to outcompete peers for limited spots pit classmates against each other, increase pressure past the optimal range, and make every assignment a potential threat to the larger goal.

When a student’s identity is rooted in achieving a prestigious outcome, setbacks become threats to the self rather than information about performance—producing exactly the fragility and avoidance that undermine genuine learning.

Motivation built on performance goals presents as high engagement when things go well, but collapses under challenge or completion—the student quits once they have arrived, or disengages when the goal feels threatened.

The alternative is not easier goals but wiser ones: definitions of success that are within the student’s influence, growth-oriented, and connected to the intrinsic value of learning rather than to where learning might lead.
quotes: A lot of times, the students who present as highly motivated in school are actually very poorly motivated for learning.
They are scarce. Each of these goals requires students to compete for limited spots. This increases pressure on students, often past what is optimal.

They emphasize and external locus of control. What I mean is, success at these goals depends to a large degree on factors outside an individual student’s influence rather than their own actions and choices.
Goals like this tend to blind us toward the beauty and power of today. Always looking to the future is a sad way to live. Ask a guy who had to learn this the hard way!

When things are going their way, sure — they’ll present as motivated for the work of learning. But this motivation will be hollow because they’ll be doing the work for where it gets them and not for the work’s inherent Value.

It takes careful, consistent heart-gardening on the part of teachers. It takes a light touch, too. We don’t want to denigrate goals like this because, c’mon — these are hard things to accomplish and we do hard things!
learning, fundamentally, is about exploring the cosmos and becoming a human.
